title: John Baptist de La Salle (7 April)
hook: a wealthy canon who gave up his comfort to start free schools for poor boys

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent Ferrer, the Dominican whose pulpit was the road. Your line was walking preacher. Where did your feet do the talking? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

A young priest in Reims has the kind of life people envy. A rich family, a fine house, a seat as a canon at the cathedral, good dinners, good books. Then he agrees to help a man who wants to open schools for poor boys, the kind who spend their days in the street. He'll just give a bit of advice. Then he'll find the teachers a place to stay. Then, because they're struggling, he invites them to eat at his own table. His family is appalled. These men are rough, untrained, poorly paid. He keeps saying yes, one small step at a time. Today, how a favor became a life.
screen: `A CANON WITH AN ENVIABLE LIFE.` → `JUST A LITTLE HELP.` → `TEACHERS AT HIS TABLE.`

segments.voice: John Baptist de La Salle later said that if he had known where those first steps would lead, he might never have taken them. But he took them. Step by step, he brought the teachers into his own house to live. Then he gave up his post at the cathedral. Then, tradition says, during a time of hunger, he gave away his family fortune to the poor, so that he would stand where his teachers stood, with nothing to fall back on. Out of that household came a community: the Brothers of the Christian Schools. They were not priests. They were laymen who made vows and gave their lives to one thing, teaching poor children, for free. La Salle changed how the teaching was done. Lessons in the children's own language, French, instead of Latin. Children grouped by what they knew, and taught together, not one at a time while the rest waited. And training for the teachers themselves, so that a teacher was not just whoever could be found, but someone formed for the work. He also wrote for his brothers about the inner side of teaching: that a classroom is a place where God is present, and that the brothers should recognize Jesus in the poor children in front of them. The prophet Daniel has a line about teachers, in the Douay-Rheims: "they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity." The Church later named La Salle patron of teachers. It began with a few hungry teachers at his table.
screen: `ONE SMALL STEP AT A TIME.` · `HE GAVE UP HIS POST AND HIS FORTUNE.` · `BROTHERS WHO TAUGHT POOR CHILDREN FREE.` · `A NEW WAY TO RUN A CLASSROOM.` · then, large: `AS STARS FOR ALL ETERNITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one teacher who changed something for you. A schoolteacher, a coach, a grandparent at a kitchen table, a boss who took time to show you how. See their face. Remember one specific thing they did: a sentence, a second chance, a moment they didn't give up. Now plan the thank-you: a message, a card, a call, or, if they've died, a word said to someone who knew them. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, just let the gratitude be real. The bell holds the time.
John Baptist de La Salle. A canon of Reims who gave up his comfort and fortune to found brothers who taught poor children for free.

segments.voice: Your line: patron of teachers. Today, send your thank-you, and be patient with one person who is learning something from you. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics keep John Baptist de La Salle's memorial on 7 April; the De La Salle Brothers and their schools honor him as their founder.
